subject: Inference access paths: trade-offs between VPC Peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN
messages:
From: ben_carter <ben.carter@redwoodinference.com>

Cc: marissa_cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>, karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Inference access paths: trade-offs between VPC Peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN

Alex / Sam,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. Per our call: GreenHealth will host an on-prem network that must access a private Redwood deployment sitting in your AWS account (private-control-plane + inference nodes). You asked for an architectural comparison so you can include it in your security review and procurement notes.

Attached are the initial diagrams and a rough cost model. High level tradeoffs we want you to consider:
- VPC Peering: simplest for high-throughput east-west traffic but no transitive routing and requires peering per VPC (cross-account peering is supported). Good for low-latency bulk token streams but has limits across regions.
- AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints): provides private IP access to a service endpoint from your VPC without exposing public IPs; great for cross-account least-privilege connections and avoids route table peering complexity. Exposes single or multi-AZ ENIs on our service side; recommended if your compliance team wants non-transitive, endpoint-level access control.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPSec / BGP): works for on-prem to cloud with encrypted tunnels, easier to operate with existing WAN, but higher latency, variable throughput, and ongoing tunnel maintenance; may be best as a fallback/burst path.

Key constraints you called out: no public internet egress for model payloads, packet inspection + IDS required on your side, and 10 Gbps sustained throughput for peak inference bursts across a multi-AZ deployment.

Request: can you confirm which of these constraints are hard vs. negotiable? I'll loop in Karthik with a short technical evaluation and cost/operational note.

Thanks,
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Ben — thanks for the summary and the diagrams. A few clarifications from our security team:
- All model payloads must remain within our controlled network (i.e., no public egress).
- We prefer mutual TLS for service authentication if possible.
- We have an existing MPLS backbone between our data centers and a preferred vendor; we can front a VPN or terminate PrivateLink from the cloud edge.

Operational asks:
- Can you provide expected 99th percentile latency for a 1-token response and for a 512-token generation over each connectivity option?
- Any special MTU or fragmentation concerns if we tunnel over our WAN?

Also, procurement will want a short note on expected monthly egress costs and any per-hour endpoint charges (for PrivateLink).

From: karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Inference access paths: trade-offs between VPC Peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN

Alex / Ben / Marissa — quick technical readout based on our infra benchmarks and GreenHealth constraints. I'll call out performance, security posture, ops complexity, and costing.

1) Performance (latency & throughput) - measured from our US-west-2 inference fleet to a customer VPC in same region:
- VPC Peering: 1-token p50~6ms p99~12ms, 512-token stream median throughput ~2500 tokens/s per r5/g4nn-like instance (no NAT hop). Best raw latency for sustained bulk streaming.
- PrivateLink: 1-token p50~8ms p99~16ms, 512-token stream throughput ~2200 tokens/s. Slight extra hop due to ENI and NLB / endpoint handling; predictable and stable across AZs.
- S2S VPN (IPSec over customer WAN): 1-token p50~20-40ms p99~60-120ms depending on MPLS hop count and current tunnel load; throughput depends heavily on tunnel capacity and CPU offload on gateways (can saturate at 300-1000 Mbps without specialized appliances).

Notes: PrivateLink adds per-connection costs and per-GB data processing charges (AWS/Cloud provider). VPC Peering has no per-hour endpoint fee but can incur cross-account data transfer charges in some regions. VPN has lowest per-GB provider cost but higher operational overhead and much higher tail latency.

2) Security / compliance
- VPC Peering: traffic is private inside provider network; however peering does not stop you from routing to other peered VPCs if not carefully controlled. No TLS termination by default; we recommend mTLS between client and Redwood service inside the tunnel.
- PrivateLink: provides the strongest network-level isolation for cross-account access — the customer never places routes to our subnet, only to an endpoint. It fits well with your 'no public egress' requirement and is easier to audit.
- S2S VPN: encryption in transit is fine, but there is more attack surface (on-prem gateway) and tunnel churn; IDS placement and packet capture usually reside on-prem which meets your inspection requirement.

3) Ops complexity and scaling
- Peering: simple for single account and single region. If GreenHealth plans multiple VPCs or regions, peering ramps up operationally (dozens of peering connections). No auto-failover: need replicates in each region.
- PrivateLink: requires you to create endpoints in each VPC you want to connect; scales better cross-account and with multiple VPCs. Also supports AWS endpoint policies for fine-grained access control.
- VPN: easy to prototype and for on-prem connectivity, but for 10 Gbps sustained traffic you'll need high-end appliances and active/active tunnels; also more maintenance windows.

4) Practical recommendation (short):
- Primary path: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) for production traffic across account boundary — meets audit/least-privilege needs and avoids complex peering mesh. Use mTLS at the application layer plus endpoint policies.
- High-throughput option: For intra-cloud same-account, same-VPC deployments where extremely low latency is required, VPC Peering is preferable (no endpoint fees).
- Fallback / burst: S2S VPN for on-prem burst or DR connectivity, or for initial PoC while endpoints are being configured.

Attached: a small BGP / IPSec snippet for your infra team (s2s_bgp_config_snippet.txt) and a quick cost model for PrivateLink vs peering (redwood_privatelink_cost_model.xlsx).

If GreenHealth wants, we can set up a 48-hour perf test from your on-prem gateway to a pinned Canary instance in our private deployment to capture real p50/p99s for your path. Let us know target window.

— Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Alex / Sam — appreciate the quick review and the constraints. Recap + next steps: 
- Recommendation: implement PrivateLink endpoints in your Cloud VPCs as the primary production access path (endpoint policies + mTLS).
- For the on-prem -> cloud connectivity (your MPLS), stand up an active/active IPSec pair as a burst/fallback path; we will not route production traffic over VPN unless endpoint capacity is exceeded.
- Ben (Redwood) will schedule a 48-hour pilot in us-west-2 next week (Aug 17-18) if that works for your infra team for perf verification. We'll provide a test plan and ephemeral endpoints.

Action items:
- Alex / Samantha: confirm pilot window and provide contact for on-prem gateway person.
- Marissa: prepare a short procurement note outlining monthly PrivateLink endpoint fees + expected data transfer estimate (use Karthik's cost model as baseline).
- Karthik: share any additional MTU or TCP tuning notes for MPLS (if non-standard values are required).

If there are no objections from your compliance team we can move to SOW drafting.

Thanks,
Ben
